newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's LDP likely to form minority government.
newsitem.headline: Japan's LDP likely to form minority government.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's party looks set to form a minority government after failing to lure potential partners into a new coalition, party officials said on Wednesday.

Although Hashimoto is assured of re-election as prime minister when parliament reconvenes on November 7, his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) has all but given up efforts to renew the outgoing coalition, officials of the Social Democratic Party said.

The LDP's partners in the old coalition, the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake party, have refused to enter into a renewed coalition, saying they feared they would become minor, irrelevant partners in a bloc dominated by the LDP.
The Social Democrats saw their strength halved in the October 20 general elections, from 30 in the outgoing Lower House to 15, while Sakigake lost seven seats to finish at just two.
The LDP won 239 seats, up from 211, but was still 12 seats short of a majority.
In lieu of a coalition, the LDP will try to retain a loose alliance with the two parties by setting up a policy forum outside the cabinet, LDP officials said.
This arrangement is to be formalised in a meeting of the three party heads on Thursday, Social Democrat sources said.
The LDP and Social Democrats remain far apart on Social Democrat proposals to ban all political donations from private firms and cut back U.S. troops on the southern island of Okinawa.
"We expect these issues to be listed in the 'no agreement' category in tomorrow's document, to be approved by the party heads," a Social Democratic source said.

The three parties, however, have agreed on moves to trim the bloated bureaucracy, on reviews of the new electoral system and women's issues, and on a common understanding of Japan's actions in World War Two based on former Prime Minister Tomiichi Murayama's 1995 expression of remorse.
It was not clear how smoothly the new alliance system would work, given the Japanese political habit of haggling among parties.
A minority government can obviously easily fall through a vote of no-confidence, which in turn would mean early general elections.
Hashimoto can also dissolve the Lower House anytime before the term ends in October 2000.
The LDP was set to start a further round of policy talks on Thursday with a fourth party, the Democrats led by reformist Naoto Kan, and with independents on Friday, LDP officials said.
But aside from a handful of independents, the LDP had little hopes of luring enough lawmakers to form a majority coalition, parliamentary insiders said.
